meta.programme: GGU DBA in Emerging Technologies (Generative AI), Cohort 8
meta.thesis: Managers already have strategy maps, OKRs and AI governance. The open question is whether evidence they can inspect shows that a delegated agent's actions are **warranted by strategy and human mandates**. I propose to design that check and **test it fairly against current practice**.
meta.purpose: This study will **design, demonstrate and evaluate** a Hybrid Alignment Diagnostic for managers who assess delegated AI-agent workflows against strategy and human mandates.

levels.name: Enterprise strategy
levels.desc: Priorities, strategy maps, OKRs at company level

levels.name: Unit and group priorities
levels.desc: What a business unit or team is asked to deliver

levels.name: Individual priorities and mandates
levels.desc: What a person may decide, approve or delegate

levels.name: AI-agent goals, instructions, guardrails

mechanisms.name: Goal / specification mismatch
mechanisms.rule: Needs a documented strategic referent **and** the agent's actual objective. A poor result alone is not enough.
mechanisms.requirement: Make goal translations and trade-offs traceable from L1 to L4.
mechanisms.example: The unit priority is timely resolution within approved commercial rules. The agent's instruction says 'close tickets fast'. The rule is missing from L4.

mechanisms.name: Information asymmetry
mechanisms.rule: Needs a **specific** missing trace or intervention point, not a generic claim that AI is opaque.
mechanisms.requirement: Separate missing evidence from real misalignment. Missing stays 'unknown'.
mechanisms.example: The action log exists, but the approval log for exceptions is not kept. The state is unknown, not misaligned.

mechanisms.name: Authority misfit
mechanisms.rule: Compares **delegated rights** with **actual permissions and actions**.
mechanisms.example: A person may approve discounts up to a limit. The agent's permission allows any discount, and the log shows one above the limit.

mechanisms.name: Accountability ambiguity
mechanisms.rule: Asks who could **approve, monitor and remedy** an outcome. A named owner is not enough.
mechanisms.requirement: Require an owner with the capacity to intervene.
mechanisms.example: The workflow names an owner, but the owner cannot reverse the agent's actions. Compare the Air Canada tribunal case: the firm stayed accountable.

mechanisms.name: Trust miscalibration
mechanisms.rule: Needs evidence about **appropriate reliance**, not a trust rating.
mechanisms.example: Reviewers approve every agent proposal without opening it. High satisfaction does not show appropriate reliance (Buçinca et al., 2021).

mechanisms.name: Coordination conflict
mechanisms.rule: Concerns conflicts at **hand-offs** between humans and agents, or agent and agent.
mechanisms.example: A pricing agent and a service agent apply different exception rules to the same customer.

method.intro: Design science builds an artefact and tests it against criteria that can fail. This page is the map an examiner asks for: every sub-problem has an objective, a question, a proposition, data and a test.
method.dsrm_note: Peffers et al. (2007). Two build–evaluate cycles planned with FEDS (Venable et al., 2016). t0 = IRB clearance; the plan runs to t0 + 9 months.
method.interfaces: Horizontal interfaces: human ↔ agent hand-offs and agent ↔ agent coordination. The cascade is a provisional design vocabulary, not a validated universal hierarchy.
method.paradigm: **Pragmatism with a design orientation.** The study judges the artefact by warranted use, comparison with a strong existing baseline, and evidence that others can inspect. Its knowledge is prescriptive: design principles that work, fail or need another test.

demo.title: A leader uses the diagnostic on one workflow
demo.intro: This is slide 9 in slow motion. It shows **how** a leader would use the diagnostic. The organisation, records and outcomes are invented. Nothing here is a study result, and the existing review may reach the same decision.
demo.workflow: An invented B2B service firm uses a **service-request agent**. It resolves customer requests and can offer goodwill credits.

chain.text: Reliable service under approved commercial rules
Service unit: timely resolution of customer requests
Team lead's mandate: credits above the limit need approval
Agent instruction: resolve requests; may issue credits

demo.use: If an examiner asks 'how would a manager actually use this?', walk through these six steps in 90 seconds. Say 'illustrative' twice. End on the action, not on a score.

steps.title: Start from the decision, not the dashboard
steps.text: The leader asks one question: are this agent's credit decisions warranted by strategy and by the team lead's mandate? The unit of analysis is one bounded workflow, not the enterprise.
steps.callout: Name the workflow, the agent and the human mandate before looking at any log.

steps.title: Build the evidence register
steps.text: The leader lists the records that each level needs. Missing records stay visible. They are never filled in by assumption.
table: Approval log for credits above the limit
steps.callout: Ask the system owner for the approval log. Do not guess.

steps.title: Apply the six evidence rules
steps.text: Each mechanism has its own rule. The output is an evidence state, not a single score.
table: Instruction omits the commercial rule that L1 requires
No approval log for large credits
Permission allows any credit; mandate sets a limit
Owner named, but cannot reverse a credit
No second agent in this workflow

steps.title: One credit above the limit: three possible branches
steps.text: The log shows one credit above the team lead's limit. The leader's decision depends on the evidence, not on the flag.
table: A documented approval for this trade-off
Records it and closes the item
Requests the evidence before any finding
The action exceeded the delegated authority
Escalates an M3 finding to an owner who can remedy it
steps.callout: Missing approval evidence means unknown. It does not prove an unauthorised action.

steps.title: The same evidence, given to the current review
steps.text: The study gives the existing strategy review and AI governance the same records and the same time. The current review may reach the same decision. That would be a valid finding: DP4 would stay unmet in that workflow.
table: Is the credit limit in the agent's permissions?
Is the missing approval log visible?
Can the owner remedy the action?
steps.callout: Do not claim the diagnostic wins. The evaluation decides that.

steps.title: The leader leaves with three actions
steps.text: 1) Add the commercial rule to the agent's instructions. 2) Align the agent's permission with the mandate limit. 3) Give the owner a way to reverse credits. In the study, the researcher records whether these findings were warranted and whether the baseline also found them.
steps.callout: End on the action list. That is what 'useful to a manager' means here.

craft.intro: These are coach practices for delivery, not Dr Sumitra's rules. Her method decides **what** you say. This page helps with **how** you say it in 12 minutes.

sections.title: The first 30 seconds
sections.lead: Examiners decide early whether you know your problem.
items: Start with the problem sentence, not with 'Good morning, my name is'. Your title slide shows your name.
Say the purpose in one breath: design, demonstrate and evaluate.
Look at the chair for the first sentence and the room for the second.

sections.title: Tell them where they are
items: Use the same three words throughout: **requirements**, **design**, **fair test**.
Begin each slide with its message, then the detail.
Before slide 4 say: 'Here is the whole study on one table.'

sections.title: Pace and pauses
items: Aim for 125–140 words per minute. Nerves push most speakers above 160.
Pause for two seconds after each slide's message.
Slow down on numbers. Say the population with every statistic.

sections.title: Use the slides, do not read them
items: Point to the table row you are speaking about.
Never read a bullet word for word.
If a slide is dense, say: 'The one thing to see here is…'

sections.title: Answer → Evidence → Limit
sections.lead: The shape of every answer in the Viva Gym.
items: Pause for two seconds before you answer. It shows thought, not doubt.
Answer in one sentence first. Then give the evidence. Then state the limit yourself.
If you do not know: 'I have not established that yet. Here is how the study would find out.'
Never defend with experience alone. Defend with evidence and design.

sections.title: When a question feels hostile
items: Thank the examiner and restate the question in one line.
Agree with the true part first: 'Yes, the existing review may be enough.'
Show that your design already allows that outcome: 'That is why DP4 can fail.'

sections.title: If something goes wrong
items: **Running long:** at 9:30, go straight to slide 9's three branches, then slide 10.
**Blank mind:** look at your anchor card. Say the slide's message sentence.
**Projector fails:** present from the PDF on your laptop or a printout.
**Mis-spoke a number:** correct it at once. 'Correction: respondents, not firms.'

sections.title: Capture the feedback well
items: Write each comment in three parts: what works, what to strengthen, one concrete fix.
Ask one clarifying question if a comment is unclear.
Fold the fixes into the topic paper the same evening.
Deck PDF on laptop, USB key and email
Cue cards printed or on your phone
One full run, then stop. Sleep.
Say the opening and the close aloud once
Charge the laptop and clicker
Water bottle in your bag
Open the deck at slide 1 in presenter view
Start the presenter timer at your first word
Breathe out slowly, twice. Then begin with the problem.

coach_tips.text: State the limit before the examiner does. It turns a weakness into evidence of rigour.
Say 'respondents', not 'companies', with every survey number.
A demonstration is not an evaluation. Say which one you mean.
Missing evidence stays 'unknown'. It never becomes a misalignment score.
The problem never names the fix. Your artefact is the answer, so it cannot be in the question.
A strong existing baseline is a reportable result, not a threat to your dissertation.
Every design proposition must be able to fail. Know which result would fail each one.

answer_checks.label: Answers the question directly
answer_checks.jev: Does the candidate's answer directly answer the examiner's question in its first one or two sentences?
answer_checks.repair: Start again with one sentence that answers the exact question. Put the reason after it.

answer_checks.label: Gives evidence (a source, a study design fact or data)
answer_checks.jev: Does the candidate's answer support its main point with specific evidence, such as a named source, a named framework, or a concrete fact about the planned study design or data?
answer_checks.repair: Add one named source or one concrete design fact, for example 'nine independent experts rate each item'.

answer_checks.label: States a real limit
answer_checks.jev: Does the candidate's answer state a substantive limitation or condition on its own main claim? A generic 'more research is needed' does not count.
answer_checks.repair: Add one sentence that starts 'The limit is…' and names a specific condition, not 'more research is needed'.

answer_checks.label: Claims no results the study does not have
answer_checks.jev: Does the candidate's answer present planned study activities, proposed thresholds or the diagnostic's performance as results that have already been achieved or proven?
answer_checks.repair: Change any 'shows' or 'proves' to 'will test'. There are no results yet.

answer_checks.label: Keeps missing evidence as 'unknown'
answer_checks.jev: Does the candidate's answer treat missing or disputed evidence as proof that the agent is misaligned?
answer_checks.repair: Say that missing evidence stays 'unknown' and that you would request the record before any finding.

slide.label: Presents proposed work as achieved results
slide.q: Does the text say that study data were collected, that experts rated items, that the diagnostic was validated, or that results were obtained?

slide.label: Claims nobody has studied the topic
slide.q: Does the text claim that the topic is unstudied, that no prior research or tool exists, or that existing frameworks completely fail?

slide.label: Treats missing evidence as proof of misalignment
slide.q: Does the slide text or script treat missing or disputed evidence as proof of misalignment?

slide.label: Generalises controlled accuracy to the field
slide.q: Does the slide text or script generalise controlled-case precision or recall to field sensitivity or enterprise-wide accuracy?

slide.label: Presents a forecast as an observed fact
slide.q: Does the text state a forecast or prediction about the future as if it were an observed, current fact?

slide.label: Names pragmatism and its consequence for evidence
slide.q: Does the slide text or script name pragmatism as the proposed paradigm and explain what it means for the evidence the study accepts?

slide.label: Grounds a feature in a kernel theory
slide.q: Does the slide show how a named kernel theory grounds a requirement, a design principle and a feature?

slide.label: Each row's data permit its test
slide.q: For each row of the traceability table, do the named data permit the named test to answer that row's research question?

slide.label: Propositions have pre-set decision rules
slide.q: Does the slide test stated artefact properties against decision rules that are fixed before evaluation?

slide.label: Walk-through labelled illustrative
slide.q: Does the slide clearly label the leader walk-through as illustrative and not a result of the proposed study?

slide.label: Problem stated without naming the fix
slide.q: Does the slide state the business problem without naming the proposed diagnostic as the solution?

answer.label: Answers the question directly
answer.q: Does the model answer directly answer the examiner's question?

answer.label: States a substantive limit
answer.q: Does the model answer admit at least one specific weakness, boundary or condition of its own claim, more specific than 'more research is needed'?

answer.label: Claims achieved results
answer.q: Does the model answer state that any study data, expert ratings, validation, pilot outcome or performance result already exists?

answer.label: Missing evidence treated as proof
answer.q: Does the model answer treat missing or disputed evidence as proof of misalignment?

deck.label: Problem before solution
deck.q: Does the storyline establish the problem and the gap before it presents the proposed diagnostic?

deck.label: Problem → gap → questions → framework → method → contribution
deck.q: Does the storyline move from problem to gap, research questions, conceptual framework, method and contribution in that order?

deck.label: Claims validation already done
deck.q: Does the storyline claim that the diagnostic has already been validated or proven effective?

slides.title: Designing a Hybrid Alignment Diagnostic
slides.subtitle: A design science proposal for bounded delegated agent workflows in India-based B2B service organisations.
slides.message: Managers need evidence to judge whether delegated agent actions fit strategy and human mandates.
script: I am Sanjay Gupta. My proposed setting is India-based B2B service organisations using tool-using agents. Managers need to judge whether delegated actions fit strategy and human mandates. Available evidence may not support that judgement.

I propose to design, demonstrate and evaluate a Hybrid Alignment Diagnostic for three bounded workflows. I will test its limits against existing practice. This is a proposal, with no evaluation results yet.
slides.transition: I will start with the assessment context.
lens: Identify the setting, technology and business uncertainty (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 1).
State the problem before proposing the artefact (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 2).
Name the design, population and setting in the purpose (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 4).
pitfalls: Do not claim unconfirmed professional experience or field success.
Coach practice: pause after the business problem before stating the purpose.

slides.title: Existing alignment tools give delegated workflows a starting point
bullets: **Problem:** Managers delegate agent actions; they should verify strategic warrant, but whether records support judgement remains unknown.
Strategy maps, OKRs, alignment maturity and NIST provide existing assessment resources.
McKinsey 2026 survey: **40%** of respondents from >US$1bn organisations scale agents; previously **27%**.
Smaller-organisation respondents: **22%**, unchanged; adoption is context, not local misalignment evidence.
slides.note: McKinsey & Company, 2026: survey, 1,719 respondents, May–June 2026; Tabassi, 2023.
slides.message: Agent adoption makes assessment timely, but does not establish local misalignment or failure of existing tools.
script: Managers delegate agent actions and should judge their strategic warrant. The uncertainty is whether available records support that judgement. I have not confirmed this problem locally. Existing alignment and governance tools provide starting points.

McKinsey and Company, 2026, reports 40% of respondents from organisations above one billion US dollars in annual revenue scaling agents, previously 27%. Smaller-organisation respondents remain at 22%. I use adoption as context, not evidence that local reviews fail.
slides.transition: I will now identify the bounded evidence gap.
lens: Use dated evidence with its population and limitations (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 1).
Keep context directly connected to the business problem (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 2).
pitfalls: Do not turn survey respondents into a census of firms or misalignment cases.
Do not use adoption or trust concern as proof that existing reviews fail.

slides.title: The gap is warranted assessment against serious existing alternatives

columns.head: RQ1 · Requirements
items: Delegation supports evidence rules (Baird & Maruping, 2021).
Governance already includes alignment (Mäntymäki et al., 2022).
Research gap: warranted rules and local comparative performance remain unresolved.

columns.head: RQ2 · Representation
items: Strategic fit informs relationships (Henderson & Venkatraman, 1993/1999).
Existing diagnostics are rivals (Diab, 2021; Issa et al., 2026).
Practitioner gap: actionable judgements from available records remain unconfirmed.

columns.head: RQ3 · Evaluation
items: FEDS separates evaluation purposes/settings (Venable et al., 2016).
Behaviour matters beyond ratings (Buçinca et al., 2021).
Hybrid performance is task-dependent (Vaccaro et al., 2024).

slides.note: Tabassi, 2023; Murray et al., 2021; Alfaify & Almarzooq, 2025. Close full-text review remains open.
slides.message: The inspected literature leaves evidence rules and comparative performance in this setting unresolved.
script: I organise the literature around three questions: requirements, representation and evaluation. Baird and Maruping, 2021, grounds delegated rights and actions. NIST already links AI goals with mission. Governance alignment is therefore not a new obligation.

For representation, strategic fit and conjoined agency offer useful starting points. Diab assesses maturity from management ratings. Issa and colleagues, 2026, already offer an Accountability Tracing Log and a preliminary delegation diagnostic. Its proxy measures, equal weights and hypothetical demonstrations leave field performance open. I must read the closest full texts before fixing novelty.

For evaluation, FEDS separates purpose from setting. Evidence on inappropriate reliance warns me that favourable ratings are insufficient. Experimental human–AI findings are task-dependent; I cannot assume hybrid superiority.

The literature tells us how alignment and governance are framed, but not whether these combined resources warrant assessment in the proposed workflows. The research gap concerns evidence rules and comparative performance. The practitioner gap concerns reaching inspectable, actionable judgements with available records. Neither is an established local failure.
slides.transition: I connect those uncertainties to three research questions.
lens: Organise literature by question, comparing support, challenge and context (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 11).
Link a research gap and a practitioner gap (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 12).
Bound novelty to inspected evidence and the proposed setting (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 12).
pitfalls: Do not claim that nobody has studied agent alignment.
Do not present an abstract's missing detail as proof of a weak full study.
Coach practice: explain one rival before describing the proposed contribution.

slides.title: Three sub-problems, three questions, one complete research chain
slides.eyebrow: SP → RO → RQ → DP → data → test
slides.note: Proposed; t0 = IRB clearance; +m = months after t0. Thresholds: slide 7. Peffers et al., 2007.
slides.message: Every sub-problem links to an objective, typed question, proposition, data and a test that can fail.
script: I start with three uncertainties, rather than three chapters. SP1 concerns unresolved evidence rules. SP2 concerns representation. SP3 concerns performance. Each has one objective and one open research question. I count deadlines from t0, the date IRB clears the instruments.

For SP1, I will produce a requirements-to-evidence matrix by month two, with expert confirmation by month five. RQ1 asks what requirements and evidence rules the assessment should meet. It is exploratory. Interviews and authorised records establish requirements; nine independent experts rate item relevance and clarity separately. DP1 requires at least eight of nine favourable ratings for each dimension.

For SP2, I will freeze v1 and produce traceable v2 by month five. RQ2 asks how to represent L1–L4 and both interfaces. It is a design question. Versions, source mappings and change logs support DP2: every requirement needs a feature and test, with at least 90% faithful audited mappings.

For SP3, I will complete evaluation by month eight. RQ3 asks how v2 performs against current practice. It is comparative. Held-out controlled cases test precision and recall. Three workflows test added value. User tasks, usability and prioritisation responses test separate properties. These criteria can fail; none establishes enterprise-wide effectiveness.
slides.transition: I will trace one proposed feature back to theory.
anchors: Data and test in every row
lens: Map each sub-problem to one objective and question (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 3).
Give objectives measurable outputs and t0-relative deadlines (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 5).
Name data and tests without empty cells (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 23).
pitfalls: Do not show an RQ→DP shortcut without the objective, data and test.
Do not move expert confirmation to month two.
Coach practice: read one complete row before summarising the other two.

slides.title: Conceptual framework: theory → requirement → feature → evaluation
slides.note: Hevner et al., 2004; Henderson & Venkatraman, 1993/1999; Murray et al., 2021; Tabassi, 2023.
slides.message: Pragmatism guides a theory-grounded design whose evidence rules and features must survive evaluation.
script: I propose pragmatism with a design orientation. I judge the artefact through warranted use, inspectable evidence and comparison with alternatives. Usefulness alone cannot establish accuracy.

Here is the M3 chain. Baird and Maruping, 2021, informs delegated rights. REQ3 requires comparing those rights with actions. DPr3 is my design principle: separate intended, authorised and observed states. The feature links mandate, permission and action records. DP2 tests faithful mapping; DP3 tests controlled performance. Evaluation feeds revision.

Strategic fit informs goal relationships. Conjoined agency informs interfaces. Responsibility analysis informs capacity to intervene. NIST is a governance framework, not a causal theory. L1–L4 is a provisional representation, including horizontal interfaces. M1 means goal/specification mismatch. The conceptual framework explains why each feature belongs.
slides.transition: I will show how the study tests this design.
lens: Name the paradigm and its evidence consequences (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 14).
Trace kernel, requirement, principle, feature and evaluation (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 8).
Keep the artefact representation distinct from research logic (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 8).
pitfalls: Do not label the L1–L4 cascade alone as the conceptual framework.
Do not equate a design rationale with validation.
Do not rename M1 as goal drift; mismatch need not involve change over time.

columns.head: Kernel → requirement
items: Pragmatism: warranted use, inspectable evidence.
Delegation: rights/actions (Baird & Maruping, 2021).
REQ3: compare delegated rights with actual actions.

columns.head: Principle → feature
items: DPr3: separate intended, authorised and observed states.
Feature: mandate ↔ permission ↔ action evidence.
L1–L4: provisional representation; include horizontal interfaces.

columns.head: Evaluation → revision
items: DP2: faithful mappings; DP3: controlled performance.
Failed rules → revision → retest.
M1: goal/specification mismatch; M1–M6 remain provisional.

slides.title: DSRM supplies six outputs; FEDS plans two build–evaluate cycles

columns.head: Define
items: 1 Identify problem → problem statement.
2 Define objectives → requirements matrix, t0+2 months.
New interviews; existing strategy and authority records.

columns.head: Construct and demonstrate
items: 3 Design/develop → v1, revision log, v2, t0+5 months.
4 Demonstrate → completed workflow assessments.
Cycle 1: artificial/formative; expert ratings and controlled tasks.

columns.head: Evaluate and communicate
items: 5 Evaluate → DP decisions, t0+8 months.
6 Communicate → dissertation and principles, t0+9 months.
Frozen-v2 held-out confirmation; Cycle 2: naturalistic/summative matched comparison.

slides.note: Peffers et al., 2007; Venable et al., 2016. New interviews/ratings/tasks; existing authorised records.
slides.message: A versioned artefact moves from requirements through formative revision to a matched naturalistic comparison.
script: I follow DSRM, the design science research methodology of Peffers and colleagues, 2007. Each activity has an output. Interviews and records establish requirements; versioned construction records why the design changes. I use expert ratings, controlled tasks and field assessment as methods inside this design.

FEDS, the framework for evaluation in design science, plans two cycles. Artificial, formative work tests v1 and supports revision. I freeze v2 before held-out artificial confirmation, then compare it in naturalistic work. Formative and summative describe purpose; artificial and naturalistic describe setting. Demonstration shows application once; evaluation tests pre-set criteria.

A survey alone measures perceptions rather than constructing this assessment. A case study can inform contextual evaluation, but my intended contribution also requires construction. Action research suits a broader participatory intervention; that would require another protocol. PLS-SEM tests construct relationships rather than the properties of this artefact.
slides.transition: I will make the acceptance and failure rules explicit.
lens: Name six DSRM activities and their outputs (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 13).
Plan evaluation separately from demonstration (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 13).
Defend the approach against plausible alternatives (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 14).
pitfalls: Do not call a walkthrough or prototype demonstration validation.
Do not say a case study cannot evaluate an artefact.
Do not choose DSR to avoid statistics.

slides.title: Acceptance criteria are separate, proposed and allowed to fail

columns.head: Content and representation
items: DP1: if ≥8/9 rate relevance/clarity separately → content criterion met.
DP2: feature/test per requirement; ≥90% faithful mappings → criterion met.
Otherwise unmet; compromised evidence → inconclusive.

columns.head: Performance and field value
items: DP3: held-out precision/recall each ≥80% → controlled criterion met.
DP4: added warranted findings in ≥2/3 workflows → criterion met.
Same evidence/time; controlled performance is not field sensitivity.

columns.head: Usability and utility
items: DP5: if SUS ≥70 → usability criterion met.
DP6: if ≥80% rate prioritisation 4–5 → utility criterion met.
Satisfaction cannot rescue failed performance.

slides.note: Proposed local thresholds; no results. Venable et al., 2016; Buçinca et al., 2021.
slides.message: Evidence for usability cannot compensate for failed fidelity, performance or warranted field value.
script: I will register these local criteria before Cycle 1. They are proposed acceptance decisions, not universal standards. If the specified evidence reaches a criterion, then that property is met. A failed property remains unmet; a compromised test may be inconclusive.

DP1 requires eight of nine experts to rate each item relevant and clear, using separate ratings. Agreement supports content, not diagnostic accuracy. DP2 requires a feature and test for every requirement, with at least 90% faithful audited mappings.

DP3 requires at least 80% controlled precision and recall on the held-out set. Precision asks what share of asserted findings is warranted. Recall asks what share of reference issues is found. I must define counting units and report raw counts. A zero denominator is undefined. These results cannot become field sensitivity.

DP4 requires additional warranted findings in two of three workflows. Both methods receive the same evidence and time. Existing review includes strategy, governance and available telemetry. Duplicates and unsupported flags do not count as added value. No qualifying gain in a valid comparison means failure.
DP5 sets a System Usability Scale score of at least seventy. DP6 requires at least 80% to rate prioritisation four or five. I report both separately from accuracy, with uncertainty.
slides.transition: These tests depend on a bounded, permissioned study.
anchors: A strong baseline can defeat DP4
lens: Fix metrics and failure decisions before testing (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 7).
Map each proposition to an evaluation episode (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 13).
Keep small-sample results descriptive with uncertainty (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 18).
pitfalls: Do not present local thresholds as universal validity standards.
Do not equate more flags, favourable ratings or controlled recall with field accuracy.
Coach practice: slow down when distinguishing precision, recall and field added value.

slides.title: The workflow is bounded; access and permission remain gates

columns.head: Chosen scope
items: 3 workflows; 1–2 India-based B2B service sites.
Workflow participants: business owners, leads, operators and governance specialists.
No prevalence, model internals or legal certification.

columns.head: People and permissions
items: 12–16 interviews/users; 9 experts; separate 3-person reference team.
Independent evaluators; relevant expertise; commitments unconfirmed.
IRB first; organisation, participant and record-use permissions separate.

columns.head: Limits → mitigations
items: Small groups → descriptive, contextual conclusions.
Withheld records → unknown; failed access → reviewed scope change.
Unread rivals → obtain full texts before fixing novelty.

slides.note: Proposed groups; access pending; no data yet. Tabassi, 2023; Hevner et al., 2004.
slides.message: Three workflows support contextual evaluation only after access, independence and permissions are secured.
script: I choose three tool-using workflows in one or two India-based B2B service organisations. I vary discretion, consequences, vendor dependence and hand-offs. At least one workflow stays outside v1 construction.

I recruit people with direct workflow responsibility, independent experts and a separate reference team. Their roles and counts are proposed; commitments and budget remain open. All participant contact and collection follow IRB clearance and organisational permission. Individual consent and record-use permission are separate.

My scope excludes prevalence, legal certification and private model reasoning. Small groups limit transfer; I report contextual evidence. Withheld records remain unknown. Failed access requires reviewed scope change, not a synthetic field substitute.
slides.transition: I will illustrate one permissioned assessment decision.
lens: Give participant roles, counts, inclusion and independence (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 15).
Clear instruments and permissions before collection (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 16).
Separate chosen boundaries from constraints and mitigations (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 9).
pitfalls: Do not call organisational access participant consent.
Do not treat withheld evidence as misalignment.
Do not replace a failed field-access gate with an undeclared synthetic pilot.

slides.title: A leader inspects evidence, preserves unknowns and chooses an action

columns.head: Same illustrative evidence
items: Enterprise: reliable service; unit: timely resolution under approved rules.
Mandate: approve exceptions; agent objective: resolve requests.
Both methods: identical mandate, permission, action and approval records.

columns.head: Evidence → decision
items: Documented authorised trade-off → no mismatch on this criterion.
Approval evidence missing → unknown; request evidence.
Sufficient evidence of action outside authority → warranted M3 finding.

columns.head: Decision → action
items: M3: record evidence and escalate; preserve disputed interpretations.
M4: identify who can monitor and remedy.
Existing review may agree; no incremental benefit established.

slides.note: Illustrative — no study results. Baird & Maruping, 2021; Santoni de Sio & Mecacci, 2021.
slides.message: The evidence rule distinguishes an authorised trade-off, an unknown approval and a warranted authority mismatch.
script: I will use an invented service workflow, not study data. The enterprise wants reliable service under approved commercial rules. The unit wants timely resolution. The human mandate requires approval for exceptions. The agent is instructed to resolve service requests.

I give the existing review and the diagnostic the same mandate, instruction, permission, action and approval records. I do not hide evidence from the baseline or assume it misses a problem. The leader starts by comparing the action with the documented authority.

If records show an authorised trade-off, there is no mismatch on that criterion. If approval evidence is missing, the state is unknown. The leader requests that evidence rather than scoring a failure. If sufficient records establish action outside authority, the leader records a warranted M3 finding and escalates it.

The rule is a threshold of evidence, not an aggregate alignment score. I preserve contradictory interpretations and record the source version. I also apply M4: who can monitor and remedy the outcome? A named owner without that capacity is insufficient. The existing review may reach exactly the same decision. Only later comparison can establish added value, and it may establish none.
slides.transition: I will close with the proposed contributions and panel questions.
lens: Demonstrate a feature's requirement and evidence rule (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 8).
Keep illustration distinct from evaluation against criteria (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 13).
Bound the practical claim to the available evidence (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 10).
pitfalls: Do not invent a baseline miss or an improvement figure.
Do not treat absent approval evidence as proved unauthorised action.
Coach practice: pause at each evidence branch before naming the action.

slides.title: A proposed instrument and conditional design knowledge

columns.head: Practice
items: Hybrid Alignment Diagnostic: instrument, evidence register, interpretation guide.
Managers inspect warranted findings and choose responsible next steps.

columns.head: Knowledge
items: Conditional design principles; successful and failed tests.
No evaluation results yet; transfer requires another bounded test.

columns.head: Questions for the panel
items: Is this bounded comparative DSR scope appropriate?
What evidence and error costs justify the proposed thresholds?

slides.note: Proposed outputs, not achieved benefits. Hevner et al., 2004; Peffers et al., 2007; Venable et al., 2016.
slides.message: The study proposes an assessment instrument and conditional knowledge about which design choices work, fail or need further evaluation.
script: I propose two contributions. Practice receives an assessment instrument, evidence register and interpretation guide for bounded workflows. Scholarship receives conditional design knowledge about preserving intent, evidence uncertainty and effective responsibility. Failed criteria and a sufficient existing baseline are reportable findings.

I have no evaluation results yet. Access, independence, closest prior art and threshold justification remain open. Another setting would require its own requirements and comparison. I welcome feedback on two decisions. Is this bounded comparative DSR scope appropriate? Which evidence and error-cost justification would make the proposed thresholds defensible?
lens: Distinguish practical artefact from scholarly design knowledge (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 10).
State contributions within the eventual evidence limits (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 9).
Defend why the proposed method is needed (Researcher's Journey, DSR step 14).
pitfalls: Do not promise a trusted instrument or proven transfer before evaluation.
Do not reopen multiple competing topics in the closing slide.
Coach practice: stop after the two panel questions and record the feedback.

questions.q: What is the actual business problem, without naming your solution?
questions.a: Managers need to judge whether delegated agent actions are warranted by enterprise priorities and human mandates. The uncertainty is whether available evidence supports that judgement.
questions.e: Tabassi (2023) already connects AI goals with mission and business value. Baird and Maruping (2021) provide the delegation perspective; the proposal examines mandates, permissions and actions.
questions.l: I have not established that this problem occurs in a participating organisation. Access and authorised workflow records must confirm the local need before the design is committed.
questions.trap: The diagnostic is the business problem.

questions.q: Where does this happen, whom does it affect, and how much does it cost?
questions.a: The proposed setting is India-based B2B service firms; affected users are business, operations and governance managers; local costs are unknown, not estimated. I plan three workflows across one or two access-pending firms.
questions.e: The paper proposes interviews and strategy, authority, instruction and action records to establish their assessment needs. Santoni de Sio and Mecacci (2021) explain why responsibility requires capacity to respond.
questions.l: Site access, affected workflows and local losses are unconfirmed. I cannot provide a defensible cost estimate or claim enterprise-wide financial harm from the current evidence.
questions.trap: Agent adoption proves losses in the proposed organisations.

questions.q: Why now? Do your adoption statistics prove misalignment?
questions.a: Adoption makes the assessment question timely; it does not prove misalignment.
questions.e: McKinsey & Company (2026) reports: 40% of respondents from organisations above US$1 billion scaled agents, versus 27% previously; smaller organisations remained at 22%. Capgemini Research Institute (2025) reports a vendor-survey trust concern. Gartner (2025) provides a forecast.
questions.l: These are different populations and evidence types. They do not estimate failure in my proposed sites, establish causation, or show that existing reviews are inadequate.
questions.trap: Adoption percentages measure agent misalignment across all firms.

questions.q: Did you actually try OKRs, strategy maps, alignment maturity and NIST before proposing another tool?
questions.a: I have examined these approaches in the literature, but have not tested their adequacy in a participating workflow. Adaptation may be sufficient.
questions.e: Henderson and Venkatraman (1993/1999), Luftman (2000), Kaplan and Norton (2004), Rompho (2024) and Tabassi (2023) provide substantial alignment and governance resources. The proposed field comparator combines existing review with available telemetry.
questions.l: The literature does not justify claiming that these approaches exclude agents. Their actual coverage and effort must be established against the same workflow evidence.
questions.trap: OKRs and governance frameworks cannot assess agents.

questions.q: What is novel compared with Issa's agentic-loafing diagnostic and Accountability Tracing Log?
questions.a: Novelty is provisional: the candidate contribution concerns warranted cross-level workflow assessment and comparative evaluation, rather than merely recording delegated accountability.
questions.e: Issa et al. (2026) already provide direct agent-specific prior art, including an Accountability Tracing Log. The paper identifies proxy measures, equal weights and hypothetical demonstrations as limits of the inspected work.
questions.l: Those limits do not establish that my design is superior. Close full texts and the proposed setting must be examined before novelty is frozen; an adaptation may be the better outcome.
questions.trap: No agent-specific diagnostic exists.

questions.q: What if the ADIPEC strategic-orchestration paper already solves your problem?
questions.a: I would revise the novelty claim and test whether adaptation or a narrower evaluation contribution remains justified.
questions.e: Alfaify and Almarzooq (2025) report a four-agent strategic technology orchestration system with pilot claims. The paper acknowledges that the accessible abstract lacks the sample and comparator detail needed to judge those claims.
questions.l: Missing detail in an abstract is not evidence of a weak full study. I must obtain the full paper before treating its limitations as a foundation for novelty.
questions.trap: Missing detail in an abstract proves that the prior study is weak.

questions.q: Why have organisations not already implemented this, and what is the research gap in one sentence?
questions.a: A possible explanation is sufficient existing reviews; the research gap is warranted evidence rules and comparative field performance, while actual adoption barriers remain unknown.
questions.e: Diab (2021) assesses maturity from ratings; Issa et al. (2026) demonstrate a preliminary delegation diagnostic hypothetically. Mäntymäki et al. (2022) already include strategic alignment within AI governance.
questions.l: I do not know why particular organisations have not adopted an assessment. That requires interviews and records, not speculation about managerial neglect or a claim that no suitable approach exists.
questions.trap: Organisations have no assessment because managers ignored alignment.

questions.q: What is your paradigm, and what does it change about the evidence you accept?
questions.a: I propose pragmatism with a design orientation: judge the artefact through warranted use and inspectable evaluation, while retaining failure and disagreement.
questions.e: Hevner et al. (2004) and Peffers et al. (2007) support theory-grounded construction and evaluation. The paper's design accepts interviews, records, expert ratings and comparative tasks as evidence for different properties.
questions.l: The current paper does not explicitly develop this philosophical rationale. I should add and defend it with the chair; usefulness alone cannot establish diagnostic truth or justify every evidence source.
questions.trap: Pragmatism means any useful tool is accurate.

questions.q: How can an L1–L4 hierarchy represent reciprocal delegation and conflicting principals?
questions.a: I would use L1–L4 with bidirectional and horizontal links, recording each principal's mandate, authorised trade-offs and unresolved conflicts. It remains a provisional representation.
questions.e: The paper includes horizontal human–agent and agent–agent interfaces. Baird and Maruping (2021) theorise delegation to and from artefacts; Murray et al. (2021) describe conjoined agency. Fechner et al. (2025) show triadic, reciprocal delegation in one healthcare case.
questions.l: That case does not establish the same structure in B2B services. Interviews and records may require revising the representation and preserving incompatible interpretations.
questions.trap: L1–L4 is a universally validated one-way hierarchy.

questions.q: Define misalignment. Why is an unsuccessful action not enough?
questions.a: A mismatch requires a warranted comparison between a documented referent and the agent objective, permission or action. Poor performance alone does not establish misalignment.
questions.e: The paper's M1 rule requires strategy and actual objective; M3 compares delegated rights with actions. Henderson and Venkatraman (1993/1999) provide relational alignment concepts, while Baird and Maruping (2021) ground delegation.
questions.l: Appropriate trade-offs can resemble contradiction. Missing referents or disputed interpretation must remain unknown; the assessment cannot infer private model intent or certify the whole enterprise as aligned.
questions.trap: Any unsuccessful agent action is misalignment.

questions.q: Trace one feature back to theory. Is your cascade really a conceptual framework?
questions.a: The conceptual framework should explain theory-to-feature reasoning; the cascade alone is the artefact's provisional representation.
questions.e: Baird and Maruping (2021) ground a requirement to compare delegated rights with actual actions. The design principle separates intended, authorised and observed states; the feature links mandate, permission and action evidence. Hevner et al. (2004) supports theory-grounded artefact construction.
questions.l: This trace is a design rationale, not validation. Expert requirements work, mapping audits and controlled cases must test whether the feature preserves meaning and detects warranted mismatches.
questions.trap: The cascade drawing itself establishes the conceptual framework and validates its features.

questions.q: Why DSR rather than a survey, case study, action research or PLS-SEM?
questions.a: The questions require me to design, demonstrate and evaluate an assessment. A survey or structural model alone would answer a different question.
questions.e: Hevner et al. (2004) and Peffers et al. (2007) connect the problem, artefact, demonstration and evaluation. The paper uses interviews and contextual comparison within that DSR design.
questions.l: A case study can support evaluation; it is not inherently incapable of it. Action design research may be appropriate if a host requires a broader participatory intervention, which would need a revised protocol.
questions.trap: DSR is appropriate because it avoids statistics and case studies cannot evaluate tools.

questions.q: Where are your primary data, and how does each question get answered?
questions.a: RQ1 uses new requirements interviews and expert ratings with existing records. RQ2 uses versioned design decisions and mapping audits. RQ3 uses controlled tasks and a field comparison.
questions.e: The paper specifies 12–16 interviews, nine independent experts, 24 controlled cases and three workflows with 12–16 users. Peffers et al. (2007) supplies the design sequence linking these outputs.
questions.l: These are planned data, not collected evidence. Organisational records are existing data; expert opinions cannot substitute for the proposed naturalistic comparison or establish diagnostic accuracy alone.
questions.trap: Expert opinion alone satisfies every research question.

questions.q: If you answer all three RQs, have you solved the main problem?
questions.a: The three answers would establish requirements, a traceable representation and bounded performance evidence. They would not eliminate misalignment.
questions.e: The paper maps SP1–SP3 to RO1–RO3 and RQ1–RQ3. DP1 checks item relevance/clarity, DP2 checks completeness/fidelity, and DP3–DP6 examine performance, added value, usability and prioritisation. Hevner et al. (2004) supports this artefact-and-knowledge contribution.
questions.l: Requirements can remain disputed and criteria can fail. Even successful local tests would answer only the specified workflow assessment problem, not establish general enterprise effectiveness or incident reduction.
questions.trap: Passing the propositions eliminates enterprise misalignment.

questions.q: Why these sample sizes? Are you copying an illustrative example?
questions.a: The proposed counts balance role coverage, independent review and a bounded doctoral evaluation; they are not population-power claims.
questions.e: The paper proposes 12–16 interviewees across four roles, nine independent experts, a separate three-person reference team and 12–16 pilot users. Venable et al. (2016) supports selecting evaluation episodes for the artefact properties being tested.
questions.l: The paper needs stronger explicit recruitment and size justification. These cited methods do not establish that the chosen counts are sufficient; coverage, disagreement, independence and access must be checked before commitment.
questions.trap: These sample sizes are sufficient because an illustrative example used similar counts.

questions.q: Why would your experts and adjudicators tell you that you are wrong?
questions.a: They must be independent of design decisions and able to reject items or findings. The proposal separates expert raters, reference adjudicators and pilot users.
questions.e: Nine experts assess relevance and clarity. A separate three-person team freezes controlled cases before seeing outputs. The paper's feasibility section explicitly treats independence and recruitment resources as gates; FEDS provides the evaluation planning basis (Venable et al., 2016).
questions.l: Independence is currently planned, not secured. Eligibility, conflicts, reporting relationships and recruitment funding must be documented; a friendly panel cannot establish accuracy through agreement.
questions.trap: A panel of supportive colleagues guarantees valid results.

questions.q: Is this evaluation, or just a convincing demonstration?
questions.a: Demonstration shows application; evaluation decides pre-set properties against evidence and a comparator. Both are required.
questions.e: Peffers et al. (2007) distinguishes DSRM activities, and Venable et al. (2016) separates evaluation purposes and settings. The paper proposes formative expert/controlled work, held-out confirmation of a frozen version, and naturalistic comparison against current practice with telemetry.
questions.l: An illustrative walk-through or a working prototype is not evaluation evidence. Artificial performance cannot establish field sensitivity, and naturalistic usability cannot rescue a diagnostic that generates unwarranted findings.
questions.trap: A persuasive prototype demonstration proves the diagnostic works.

questions.q: Who creates ground truth, and how do you prevent tuning to the test?
questions.a: An independent reference team freezes case keys before inspecting outputs. Twelve cases support formative work; twelve are held out for the frozen version.
questions.e: The paper explicitly specifies that separation and reserves at least one field workflow from v1 construction. Kapoor et al. (2024), a preprint, warns that benchmark accuracy can conceal overfitting and cost.
questions.l: Constructed reference cases are not complete ground truth for operational workflows. The protocol still needs explicit acceptable alternatives, disputed-case handling and adjudication rules; revision after held-out testing would require a new confirmation set.
questions.trap: Cases used to revise the artefact can also confirm that revised version.

questions.q: Why 8/9 experts, 90% mapping fidelity, 80% precision/recall and SUS 70?
questions.a: These are proposed local acceptance criteria for separate properties, not universal standards. They require justification before testing begins.
questions.e: The paper assigns each threshold to a DP and states that criteria can fail. Venable et al. (2016) supports planned evaluation; Buçinca et al. (2021) warns against equating favourable ratings with appropriate reliance.
questions.l: The paper's cited sources do not establish these exact cut-offs. Error costs, denominator rules and sponsor/chair judgement must justify them; I cannot claim that crossing them validates the entire diagnostic.
questions.trap: The numerical cut-offs are universal validity standards.

questions.q: What exactly are precision and recall, and what if a denominator is zero?
questions.a: Precision divides warranted flags by all flags; recall divides detected reference issues by all reference issues; zero denominators make the affected measure undefined.
questions.e: The paper proposes separate thresholds against frozen held-out cases. Its M1–M6 evidence rules distinguish actual warranted findings from poor outcomes or absent records; Kapoor et al. (2024) cautions against narrow benchmark claims.
questions.l: Zero denominators are undefined, not perfect performance. Small controlled sets need raw counts and uncertainty. These measures do not establish field sensitivity, population prevalence or completeness over unknown operational failures.
questions.trap: An undefined denominator means perfect performance.

questions.q: What makes the field baseline fair, and how do you avoid learning effects?
questions.a: Both approaches receive the same evidence and task budget. The baseline includes current strategy review, governance and available telemetry, not an artificially weak checklist.
questions.e: The paper requires this matched comparison and keeps a workflow outside initial construction. Existing resources include Henderson and Venkatraman (1993/1999), Tabassi (2023) and Rompho (2024).
questions.l: The current paper needs a more explicit reviewer/order assignment to expose carryover. If evidence access differs or reviewers learn from the first method, I must disclose that limitation or revise the comparison.
questions.trap: A fair comparison may give the diagnostic better records or more time.

questions.q: Suppose the diagnostic finds more flags. When does that count as added value?
questions.a: Only distinct, warranted findings beyond a valid baseline count. More unsupported flags are not added value.
questions.e: DP4 in the paper requires added warranted findings in at least two of three workflows. The proposal separates unknown evidence from mismatch and accepts a strong baseline as a reportable outcome. Venable et al. (2016) supports evaluation of the intended property.
questions.l: Three workflows provide contextual yield and effort, not a general superiority estimate. The protocol must define deduplication and adjudication; a compromised comparison is inconclusive rather than a diagnostic win.
questions.trap: More flags automatically mean more value.

questions.q: If users love it but it performs poorly, is the research successful?
questions.a: Positive usability or utility cannot rescue failed performance. Each proposition receives its own met, unmet or inconclusive decision.
questions.e: Buçinca et al. (2021) found that interventions reducing inappropriate reliance could receive less favourable ratings. Vaccaro et al. (2024) found task-dependent human–AI performance, with average combinations below the better standalone component. The paper separates DP3–DP6.
questions.l: Those studies do not estimate failure rates for this diagnostic. They justify separating subjective experience from warranted performance; they do not predict whether my particular instrument will pass or fail.
questions.trap: High usability can compensate for failed diagnostic performance.

questions.q: What would make you abandon or materially revise the diagnostic?
questions.a: A valid comparison without qualifying added value leaves DP4 unmet. Failed precision, recall or fidelity requires revising the faulty design rather than relabelling success.
questions.e: The paper explicitly permits negative findings and a sufficient existing baseline. Peffers et al. (2007) and Venable et al. (2016) support construction with planned evaluation and iteration.
questions.l: Access failure is different from an evaluated failure: it prevents the dependent conclusion. Material scope or protocol changes require review; I cannot quietly replace a field comparison with expert-only or synthetic evidence.
questions.trap: Unfavourable criteria should be reworded until the diagnostic passes.

questions.q: What happens if records are withheld or the researcher controls the host team?
questions.a: Withheld evidence remains visible as unknown. The study cannot treat a missing trace as an agent failure or rely on designer-controlled evaluation.
questions.e: The paper requires access to strategy, mandates and traces before site commitment and separates evaluators. Santoni de Sio and Mecacci (2021) supports examining capacity to respond rather than merely naming an owner.
questions.l: Host access and researcher relationships remain unconfirmed. Failed access requires revised scope; power relationships could affect candour and consent. An expert-only fallback cannot be presented as the planned field pilot.
questions.trap: A missing record proves the agent failed.

questions.q: What is the IRB route, who owns the data, and can you send records to an AI service?
questions.a: IRB clearance precedes collection; ownership remains unresolved, and confidential records cannot reach an AI service without explicit organisational, participant and record-use authorisation.
questions.e: The paper explicitly makes these permissions prerequisites and excludes legal certification and private model reasoning. Tabassi (2023) and Mäntymäki et al. (2022) provide governance context, not permission to export confidential data.
questions.l: Ownership, storage, retention and external-service permissions are not settled in the paper. I cannot infer consent from access or send confidential records to an external model without explicit authorised terms.
questions.trap: Access to records permits external AI processing without separate approval.

questions.q: Do you need an LLM for the diagnostic, and who pays if model costs rise?
questions.a: The research does not require an LLM-based diagnostic. Inspectable rules, records and comparisons may be sufficient; existing telemetry avoids new monitoring infrastructure.
questions.e: The paper defines an evidence register, instrument and interpretation guide, not a mandatory inference service. Kapoor et al. (2024) warns that agent accuracy can obscure cost; Tabassi (2023) connects AI use with business value.
questions.l: Hosting, model choice and operating costs are unconfirmed. Any automated component needs separate justification and permissions; the presentation coach's AI checks are not evidence that the research instrument requires AI.
questions.trap: An LLM is necessary because agents are the research topic.

questions.q: Walk me through a leader using it, without assuming it beats the existing review.
questions.a: In an illustrative service workflow, the leader compares strategic priority, human mandate, agent objective, permissions and an action trace. They then decide what evidence or intervention is needed.
questions.e: The paper's M3 compares rights with actions; M4 asks who can approve, monitor and remedy. Baird and Maruping (2021) grounds delegation and Santoni de Sio and Mecacci (2021) grounds effective responsibility.
questions.l: Missing approval evidence means unknown, not proved unauthorised action. The existing review may reach the same decision. This invented example illustrates use, not evaluated added value.
questions.trap: The invented walkthrough proves the diagnostic finds issues that existing reviews miss.

questions.q: What is the contribution beyond another checklist, and can it transfer?
questions.a: The intended contribution combines an assessment instrument with conditional knowledge about representations and evidence rules that work or fail in bounded workflows.
questions.e: Hevner et al. (2004) supports artefact and research contributions. The paper specifies a framework, evidence register, instrument and interpretation guide, evaluated through separate criteria. Theoretical inputs include strategic fit, delegation and conjoined agency.
questions.l: There are no tested design principles yet. Three workflows cannot establish transfer across sectors; another organisation would need to test requirements, baseline fit and the same decision rules before claiming reuse succeeds.
questions.trap: A successful local checklist transfers to every sector.

questions.q: Why should we trust your work, and what is your biggest unresolved weakness?
questions.a: Trust should rest on inspectable evidence, explicit limits, independent judgement and a design that can fail, rather than my experience or a polished prototype.
questions.e: The paper preserves unknown and disputed evidence, freezes reference cases, separates evaluators and compares against current practice. Hevner et al. (2004) and Venable et al. (2016) supply the construction and evaluation basis.
questions.l: Access, independence, close-prior-art review and exact threshold justification remain unresolved. Until those gates are secured and evaluation occurs, this is a defensible proposal, not a validated diagnostic.
questions.trap: Experience and a polished prototype are enough to trust the research.

criteria.text: State the business problem before the solution: what happens, what should happen, who is affected, what is unknown. The problem never names the fix.
Every statistic carries its source, population and evidence type. Forecasts and vendor surveys are labelled.
State the gap as 'the literature tells us X, but not Y', with one research-gap and one practitioner-gap sentence.
Never claim that nobody has studied the topic, and never use 'agents are new' as the gap. Treat close prior art as a rival.
Say the purpose in one breath with design, demonstrate and evaluate. Never 'explore'.
Each sub-problem maps to one objective (verb, number, deadline from t0) and one open, typed research question.
Each design proposition has a metric and a decision rule fixed before Cycle 1, and can fail.
Show SP → RO → RQ → DP → data → test with no empty cells.
Name the paradigm (pragmatism) and what it means for the evidence you accept.
Conceptual framework = kernel theory → requirement → design principle → feature, with the build–evaluate loop. The artefact has its own name.
Name DSRM and show its six activities, each with an output. Design is not method: name the data-collection methods inside it.
Plan evaluation with FEDS: artificial then naturalistic. A demonstration is not an evaluation.
For each participant group give role, count, inclusion and independence. Nothing is collected before IRB clearance.
Reject the alternatives (survey, case study, action research, PLS-SEM) in one sentence each.
Separate scope (your choices) from limitations (constraints); give each limitation a mitigation.
State two contributions: reusable design knowledge and the practical artefact. Do not claim results you do not have.
Show a leader using the framework on clearly labelled illustrative data: evidence, decision rule, action.
Be ready to defend every line, especially 'why this method, and do you really need it?'.
